scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.

The Arapaho entry is a people-level history, with separate northern and southern communities. It is not attached to the modern Cheyenne-Arapaho Oklahoma record, Aaniiih/Gros Ventre, every Algonquian-speaking people or every archaeological site in Colorado. Imported endpoints and geometry remain unchanged; no successor state is manufactured.

The Arapaho Project history provides broad phases, not precise early migration dates. Its apparent 1861 treaty-ratification simplification, outdated language counts and categorical contemporary cultural-decline claims are excluded. The 1492 opening is only the start of the map interval. The earliest phase openly states uncertainty and does not make European documentation the beginning of Arapaho history.

The Smithsonian catalogue records were read as text, not as direct inspections of the objects or their images. Manufacture, acquisition and publication dates are distinguished. The cradle’s named previous owner is not silently identified as its maker. The scraper belongs to a collection from five named people; the catalogue does not select one of them as its individual owner. The modern doll’s inferred Santa Fe provenance is not asserted as certain.

Hilger’s 1952 monograph was read in a public Internet Archive OCR copy after direct Smithsonian PDF access failed. The Smithsonian repository confirms publication and public-domain status. Preface xiii dates interviews with Southern Arapaho to 1935 and 1941 and Northern Arapaho to 1936, 1940 and 1942. The childhood memories, friendship accounts and baby-care material appear on printed pages 107 to 110 and 28 to 29. These are attributed recollections and observations, not unchanged practices in 1492. No images or full-book close reading is claimed.

Hilger’s account reflects an outsider researcher, translation and her selection of interviewees. Her moral judgements, essentializing claims and criticisms of young mothers are not adopted. Named speakers’ contrasting friendship accounts are retained. The baby-care paragraph reports a historical absorbent and toilet training without instructions, safety or efficacy assertions, humour at families’ expense or identifying an unnamed informant.

Hilger’s pages 29 to 31 record disagreements between Arapaho women and museum labels about all-beaded cradles. The selected NMAI cradle has a documented wooden frame, canvas and quill work; this narrative does not transfer the contested all-beaded attribution or sacred meanings to it. No private ceremonial details or claim of universal cradle symbolism is added.

The Boulder report was read for its named community representatives and Landscape section. Claims about exact horse travel range, a universal number of residents per lodge, a supposed Niwot curse, medical efficacy of plants, fish avoidance across all Arapaho communities and historic legal conclusions are not repeated. Its erroneous ten-year interval between 1851 and 1858 is not adopted. The camp item is broader context, not a newly located archaeological camp.

The Arapaho plant list supports named foods only, not their invention, first use or use in a specific map year. The item remains undated broader context because this page does not provide a secure publication or observation date. No foraging identification, dosage or medicinal efficacy is asserted.

Kelly and Cowell’s 2023 article and PDF return an access challenge directly. Its indexed abstract, introduction and figure 1 caption were read and support the 2019 session and commission collaboration. No complete paper review, image inspection, audio testing, current speaker count or quantitative language-gain claim is made. The article and PDF are treated as one work.

The tribal language page describes current initiatives. It is not evidence that all learners achieve fluency. Cheyenne and Arapaho remain distinct languages. The 2025 agriculture page supports distributions and restoration activity, not clinical outcomes or medical advice. No changing headcount, herd count or officeholder is treated as timeless.

The NPS page identifies the November 29, 1864 massacre and manuscript letter copies rediscovered in 2000. Victims are not reduced to a military defeat or treated as a vanished people. The original letters were not inspected. No graphic descriptions are reproduced.

The narrative is author-checked and awaits independent historical review. No border certification, added historical lifetime or successor relation is claimed. Later stories remain visibly separate when an early year is selected.

proposedOverrides.summary: Arapaho people continue in distinct northern and southern communities, including the Northern Arapaho Tribe at Wind River in Wyoming and Southern Arapaho members of the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma.

identityEvidence.assessment: Broad central Plains people-level outline. The imported 1492 to 1783 interval is map coverage. Neither early village distribution nor exclusive sovereignty is validated. The separate Cheyenne-Arapaho (Oklahoma) outline at 1492 is anachronistic for the later combined institution and is not attached to this card.
